Mapping / Alignment

  • Align short reads onto a reference sequence

⇒\Longrightarrow Reference sequence is necessary

Every number produced later this week is downstream of where these reads land.

Alignment/Homology Search

  • Pairwise alignment
    find the best-matching piecewise alignments of two sequences
    BLAST, Bowtie, BWA
  • Multiple alignment
    find the best-matching of more than two sequences
    ClustalW, MUSCLE, MAFFT
Pairwise compares two sequences; multiple compares many at once. RNA-seq is always the first — a million times over.

Alignment/Homology Search

Most of RNAseq aligners use

⇒\Longrightarrow Pairwise alignment

why?

because the alignment should be between a reference sequence and a short read. Usually there are a lot of short reads and it is computationally impossible to do multiple alignment for all of them.

Alignment/Homology Search

When you compare genes between species, you should use

⇒\Longrightarrow Multiple alignment

why?

because normally it is a comparison of several sequences (of genes) at the same time among several species.

Pairwise alignment

Global — the best match of the two sequences in their entirety
FTFTALILLAVAV F--TAL-LLA-AV
Local — the best match of the two sequences partially
FTFTALILL-AVAV --FTAL-LLAAV--

Global alignment has to use every residue of both sequences, so it spends score on the ends. Local alignment is free to stop, and keeps only the stretch that actually matches.

A read is short and a genome is long. RNA-seq mapping is always local.

Pairwise alignment

Most of RNAseq aligners use

⇒\Longrightarrow Local alignment

why?

because normally a reference sequence is very long and sequenced reads are very short, and the purpose of the RNAseq alignment is to find the location that the short reads coming from in the long reference sequence.

Pairwise Alignment

  • Global Alignment
    • Needleman-Wunsch method1
  • Local Alignment
    • Smith-Waterman method2



  1. S.B. Needleman et al., J. Mol. Biol., 48:443-453, 1970.
  2. T.F. Smith et al., J. Mol. Biol., 147:195-197, 1981.
Two algorithms, from 1970 and 1981. Every practical mapper is a shortcut around one of them.

Smith-Waterman

  1. Make a score matrix
  2. Trace back to get an alignment

⇒\Longrightarrow Slow but sensitive

Optimal, and far too slow for a million reads. That gap is where every real mapper lives.

Example

Why filling a table gives you an alignment

A walk across a grid. One sequence along the top, the other down the side. Start top-left, finish bottom-right.

Every step is a decision. Diagonal: these two letters are a pair. Straight across: a letter with no partner — a gap.

So the route is the alignment. Walk it, write down each step, and it is written. Every alignment there could be is one of these routes.

You never try them all. Each crossing keeps only the best way to reach itself. Fill the grid once, walk back from the best number.

top G A T T A side G A - T A

↘ a pair  ·  → or ↓ a gap

A crossing may also say start again here. That is all local means.

Smith-Waterman example (step1)

  1. Put 0 in the 1st row and 1st column
  2. Focus on i=1 (row), j=1 (col) position
  3. Calculate the following 4 values
  • Hi−1,j−1+w(a,b)=H0,0+w(A,A)=0+2=2H_{i-1,j-1} + w(a,b) = H_{0,0} + w(\text{A},\text{A}) = 0+2 = 2
  • Hi−1,j+w(a,−)=H0,1+w(A,−)=0−1=−1H_{i-1,j} + w(a,-) = H_{0,1} + w(\text{A},-) = 0-1 = -1
  • Hi,j−1+w(−,b)=H1,0+w(−,A)=0−1=−1H_{i,j-1} + w(-,b) = H_{1,0} + w(-,\text{A}) = 0-1 = -1
  • 00

and keep the largest of the four.

The fourth value is the whole of Smith-Waterman: a cell may never go below zero, so a bad stretch cannot drag a good alignment down with it.

Smith-Waterman example (step2)

  1. Compare the following 4 values
  2. Select the max value
  3. Repeat this process until all cells are filled
  4. Backtrace from the biggest value
The matrix is filled once and the alignment is read back out of it. Filling it is the expensive part.

Smith-Waterman Example

Trace back the path on the biggest score from the right bottom

  • Sequence 1 = A-CACACTA
  • Sequence 2 = AGCACAC-A
Trace back from the largest score, not from the corner. That is what makes it local.

Filling it is mechanical. Choosing the route back out of it is the part worth slowing down for — the next four slides do one step each.

Nothing here says where the alignment starts or ends. The numbers do.

The fourth option, 0, is the only difference from Needleman–Wunsch. It is a floor, and it is also where an alignment is allowed to end.

Step 1 — start at the biggest number

Not the bottom-right corner. That is Needleman–Wunsch, where the alignment has to run end to end.

Here you start at the largest value anywhere in the table — 5, at row A, column A. It happens to be in the corner this time; that is luck, not a rule.

That cell is the end of the alignment. You are about to walk backwards from it.

Largest value = best local alignment. If two cells tie, there are two equally good alignments, and the tool picks one.

This is the whole method. Three sums, one of them matches the number in the cell, and that tells you the step.

Keep going until you step onto a 0. That zero is where the alignment begins — here at row 0, column 1.

Sequence1 C A - C A Sequence2 - A G C A ^ ^ ^ ^ score 5

Four steps, read backwards: pair, pair, gap, pair. The leading C of Sequence1 never entered the route, so it is simply left out.

Local alignment does not have to use the whole read. Being allowed to stop is what lets it ignore a bad beginning.

Key Takeaways: alignment fundamentals

  • Pairwise vs Multiple: RNA-seq uses pairwise alignment (read vs reference)
  • Global vs Local: RNA-seq uses local alignment (find position in long reference)
  • Smith-Waterman: Optimal but slow → practical aligners use heuristics
Three choices, all forced by one fact: the reads are short, the reference is long, and there are millions of reads.

Why these choices?

  • Pairwise: Computationally feasible for millions of reads
  • Local: Short reads mapping to long genome/transcriptome
  • Heuristics instead of Smith-Waterman: give up the guarantee, buy the speed

A heuristic is a rule for where to look, so the search can skip the rest. Not random — run it twice and you get the same answer — just not guaranteed to be right.

Smith-Waterman is exact and too slow. Every mapper you use today is an approximation that usually — not always — agrees with it.

Next: How do we make it fast enough for millions of reads?

There are some issues

Matches & Mismatches

A real read never matches perfectly. The question is how much mismatch you are willing to pay for.

Gap & Soft trimming

Soft clipping keeps the bases in the file but out of the alignment — so the read length in a SAM file is not the aligned length.

How to map million reads?

An index is an alphabetical list of names and subjects with references to the places where they occur. Sorted, structured, and therefore fast to search.

A mapper works the same way: it looks a read up in an index of the reference — it never compares the read against the genome base by base.

Hash table (seed) Burrows–Wheeler (BWT / FM-index)
Speed slower faster
Mismatches more allowed few, typically < 3
Indels detected limited
Examples GSNAP, Novoalign Bowtie2, BWA, HISAT2

STAR sits between the two: a suffix array rather than a hash table, but the same idea of finding seeds first and extending them afterwards.

Building the index is a separate, slow, one-off step — which is why the mapping practical builds it once and everyone reuses it.

Hash table (seed) method

  1. Build the table once. Walk the genome, write down where every k-mer occurs.
  2. Look up a piece of the read — not the whole read, one short exact piece: the seed.
  3. The table hands back a few positions.
  4. Extend from each one into a full alignment. Smith–Waterman, the slow part — but on a handful of places, not everywhere.

The read is never compared against the genome — only against the few positions the table gave back.

genome — the two red blocks are positions 12 and 20

read — the red piece is the seed

SeedPositions
AAAA0, 8
GTGA12, 20
……

Two places to check, not three billion.

The seed length is the dial. Shorter seeds survive mismatches, and also turn up more often by chance, so more places come back to be extended. Sensitive and slow, or fast and fussy.

Redrawn after Flicek P & Birney E, Nature Methods supplement (2009) and Li H & Homer N, Briefings in Bioinformatics (2010).

Genome & Transcripts

Map to the genome and you can still find a junction nobody annotated. Map to the transcriptome and you can only find what is already there.

Spliced / Unspliced aligners

  1. Spliced aligners allow for the presence of introns
    BLAT, GMAP/GSNAP, STAR, HISAT2, minimap2
    ⇒\Longrightarrow Map mRNA reads to genome reference
  2. Unspliced aligners DO NOT allow for the presence of introns
    BLAST, BWA-MEM / BWA-MEM2, Bowtie2, minimap2
    ⇒\Longrightarrow Map mRNA reads to transcriptome reference

Which of these you would actually install today. BLAT and BLAST were written before short reads existed; Bowtie 1 and bwa aln have been replaced by Bowtie2 and BWA-MEM. For long reads — PacBio, Nanopore — the usual answer is minimap2, spliced with -x splice and unspliced without it. kallisto and salmon are not aligners at all: they match k-mers straight to transcripts, never produce a BAM, and cannot tell you where in the genome a read came from. You run kallisto in the counting practical.

Which aligner should be used for DNA reads alignment?

An RNA read can cross an intron; a DNA read cannot. That one fact chooses your mapper.

Seed and extend — what every mapper does

Each read is cut into k-mers and looked up in a table of the genome. Matching k-mers are then extended into a longer alignment, and the gap that opens may be an intron.

  • Little bias: the best placement for every read
  • More tolerant of sequence differences

Mappers differ in how they find the seed, not in doing this.

where the seed is foundmapper
hash table of k-mersGSNAP (the drawing above)
suffix arraySTAR
FM-index (BWT)HISAT2, BWA-MEM, Bowtie2
minimizersminimap2

Redrawn from Figure 1 of Garber M, Grabherr MG, Guttman M & Trapnell C, "Computational methods for transcriptome annotation and quantification using RNA-seq", Nature Methods 8:469–477 (2011).

Alignment algorithm overview

How the seed is found FM-index (BWT) suffix array / minimizers
Representatives Bowtie, BWA STAR, minimap2
Speed Very fast Fast
Memory usage Low High
Splice junction Not supported Well supported
Sequence divergence Best for < 2-3% Good for > 2-3%
Use case Genome mapping
Close species		 Transcriptome mapping
Distant species
There is no best mapper. There is a best mapper for your reference and for how far your reads sit from it.

Alignment-free RNA-seq quantification

  • Kallisto 2016, https://pachterlab.github.io/kallisto/
  • Salmon 2017, https://combine-lab.github.io/salmon/
No alignment at all — only whether a read's k-mers are compatible with a transcript. That is where the hundred-fold speed comes from.

de Bruijn Graph (DBG)

Read is divided by k-mer

caption = k-mer = 2

de Bruijn Graph (DBG)

Merge graphs with same nodes

The graph is built once from the transcriptome. After that a read is just a walk through it.

Pseudoalignment

It never says where in the transcript a read came from, only which transcript. For counting, that is enough.

Calculation time

On this course's data, kallisto takes about 26 seconds per sample where STAR takes four minutes. You will measure both.

Limitation of alignment-free

  • Alignment-free and alignment-based quantification methods perform similarly for common gene targets, such as protein-coding genes
  • However, we have identified a potential pitfall in analyzing and quantifying lowly-expressed genes and small RNAs with alignment-free pipelines, especially when these small RNAs contain biological variations.

https://doi.org/10.1186/s12864-018-4869-5

Alignment-free tools
Kallisto & Salmon

  • Super ultra fast > STAR, HISAT2
  • Good performance for well-constructed reference
    • Human, Mouse, Arabidopsis
  • Transcriptome reference is needed for T-DBG
    • Mis-estimation risk for a draft assembled/annotated genome/polyploid reference?

No annotation, No alignment

Alignment-free methods: limitations

  • ❌ Poor annotation dependency: Incomplete/draft annotations → inaccurate quantification
  • ❌ Low-expressed genes: Insufficient k-mer coverage affects reliability
  • ❌ Small RNAs: Short sequences with biological variations poorly handled
  • ❌ Novel junction detection: Cannot discover unknown splice variants
  • ❌ Polyploid genomes: Reference bias issues in allele-specific expression

Recommendation

Use alignment-free for: Well-annotated genomes (human, mouse, Arabidopsis) + standard RNA-seq
Use alignment-based for: Novel species, splice discovery, SNP calling, structural variants

Benchmark in polyploid genome

  • Error = classifications to the wrong subgenome / the number of read alignments
  • using A. halleri and A. lyrata RNA-seq data (n=3)
Tony Kuo and Martin C Frith and Jun Sese and Paul Horton. EAGLE: Explicit Alternative Genome Likelihood Evaluator. BMC Medical Genomics. 11(Suppl 2):28. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12920-018-0342-1
Two subgenomes sit 2–3 % apart — exactly where the fast methods start to guess.

How to select a mapper

  • Mapping tasks
    • Spliced or Unspliced
    • Genome or Transcriptome reference
  • Distance between reference and reads — a question about how the seed is found, not about the index
    • < 2–3 % divergence: a short exact seed is nearly always there — FM-index (Bowtie2, BWA) is fastest, and alignment-free (kallisto) works at all
    • > 2–3 % divergence: a fixed-length exact seed often is not — mappers that grow the seed until it breaks (STAR) keep working; alignment-free stops
All of them are seed-and-extend. Divergence decides whether a seed of the length the mapper insists on still exists — and the next slide measures it.

SAM format after mapping

  • Sequence Alignment Map format
    Single unified format for storing read alignments to a reference genome
    →\longrightarrow Text file, Human readable
  • Binary Alignment Map format
    Binary equivalent of SAM
    Developed for fast processing/indexing
    →\longrightarrow Binary file, Compressed

http://samtools.github.io/hts-specs/SAMv1.pdf

One line per alignment, not per read: a read that maps in two places appears twice.

Example SAM file

Every line is one read's story: where it went, how well, and what had to be assumed.

Structure of SAM file

  • Tab-delimited text file
  • Optional header section
  • Followed by alignment section
The header says what reference was used. A BAM without it cannot be interpreted at all.

Alignment section

Eleven mandatory fields, always in this order, then as many optional tags as the mapper wants to add.

Mandatory fields

FLAG and CIGAR carry the most information and are the hardest to read. Everything else is nearly self-explanatory.

Mapping quality score

* **SUM_BASE_Q(best):** the sum of base quality scores at mismatched bases for the best alignment * **SUM_BASE_Q(i):** the sum of base quality scores at mismatched bases for the i alignment

Mapping quality scores quantify the probability that a read is misplaced.

Li H, Ruan J, Durbin R., 2008, Genome Research 18:1851-8.

Mapping quality report Samstat

MAPQ is not base quality. It is the probability that this read is in the wrong place entirely.

CIGAR String

Compact Idiosyncratic Gapped Alignment Report

CIGAR says what happened to every base of the read: matched, inserted, deleted, skipped across an intron, or clipped away.

Mapping Visualization

IGV Integrative Genomics Viewer
http://www.broadinstitute.org/igv/home

When a number surprises you, look at the reads. Almost every surprise in this course is visible in IGV.

IGV

Coverage, mismatches and junctions in one picture. This is the fastest way to check a result you do not believe.

SNPs
Single Nucleotide Polymorphism

A column where the reads disagree with the reference and with nothing else. If only some of them disagree, look at the depth before you call it.

Insertion

An insertion is in the read and not in the reference — so it lives in the CIGAR, not in the coordinates.

Deletion

A deletion and an intron look alike in the alignment. The mapper tells them apart by length and by splice sites.

Mini Summary

  • Mapper: spliced or unspliced?, where to map: genome or transcriptome?
  • SAM file: huge amount of mapping information
  • Mapping quality: highly influences estimation of transcripts reconstruction and abundances
  • Data visualization: helpful for further inspect particularly problematic regions

Quick review sample data

From here on every example is the data you will analyse yourselves.

A. kamchatica allotetraploid

A. kamchatica carries two whole genomes at once, one from A. halleri and one from A. lyrata. Every gene comes as a pair.

Homeolog duplicated gene pair

Homolog, ortholog, paralog, homoeolog

The pair is the point. Telling the two copies apart is the whole analytical problem of this dataset.

Homeolog specific expression

If the two copies of one gene are expressed differently, that difference is inherited from two different ancestors.

Wild-type A. kamchatica resequencing

25 accessions

Twenty-five accessions is what makes this a population question rather than an anecdote.

Hydroponic chamber experiment

Hydroponics is how you control the one variable that matters. It is also why the roots and the leaves can be sampled separately.

Zinc concentration

Zinc is the treatment. Everything you will test on Wednesday is a comparison against this one contrast.

Zinc transport in A. halleri

A. halleri tolerates and accumulates zinc; A. lyrata does not. In A. kamchatica both ancestors are present in the same nucleus.

Working hypothesis

Heavy metal related genes (homeologs) are expressed higher in A. halleri subgenome than in A. lyrata subgenome in root&leaf

→\longrightarrow Test it by RNAseq

Differential homeolog expression analysis pipeline (EAGLE-RC)

EAGLE-RC: https://github.com/tony-kuo/eagle
EAGLE-RC decides, read by read, which subgenome it came from. That classification is the result, not a preprocessing step.
